stories.title: France braces for more unrest amid fresh protests
stories.summary: France will deploy a 70,000-strong police presence to contain expected unrest in the latest nationwide protests. The demonstrations are driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron's government. The nationwide demonstrations come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen. "Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble," Mr Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying "a very high risk" of unrest. Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities.

stories.title: Consumers may face higher waste charges on report advice
stories.summary: Consumers could face higher waste charges after a Government-commissioned report recommended increasing landfill and recovery levies. The long-awaited report said the two levies should each "gradually increase" by €100 per tonne and acknowledged the costs would eventually be passed on to householders. It recommended the introduction of incentivised charging to encourage separation of waste and recycling. The report by consultancy Tetra Tech said there was a "persistent gap" between Ireland's recycling rates and its targets. It said Ireland was falling far short of its EU targets, recycling just 1.3 million tonnes of the 3.1 million tonnes of municipal waste generated in 2023. This left the State exposed to infringement proceedings, possible fines, as well as other environmental and economic costs.

stories.title: Bohs comeback secures second spot ahead of St Pat's
stories.summary: Bohemians came from behind to consolidate second place in the Premier Division table as St Patrick's Athletic failed to rediscover some home comfort to end their season on a high from this thrilling Dublin derby at Richmond Park. Alan Reynolds’s Gypsies thus finish five points ahead of St Pat’s and three behind champions Shamrock Rovers. A second successive home defeat to Dublin rivals made it no win in four for St Pat’s as their promising season finished with something of a whimper, albeit with European qualification having been guaranteed. Far from a dead rubber game despite the title challenge for both having evaporated over the last fortnight, a second place finish brings a not inconsiderable financial boost to Bohs as it secures a bye into the second round of the UEFA Conference League next summer. That’s worth a minimum of €525,000 (as opposed to €325,000), in addition to slightly more in domestic prize money for runners-up over third place. Two points behind Bohs at kick-off, Saints simply had to win to leapfrog the Phibsborough side.

stories.title: Untangling the Hallowe'en story - we didn't really invent it
stories.summary: Folklorist Michael Fortune takes a deep dive into the myths and legends behind Hallowe'en... I’ve been recording and sharing content about Hallowe’en from around the country and beyond for the past 20+ years and although I spent many of these years promoting the Irish connection to Hallowe’en, I now see a lot dubious claims circulating that we invented it and it was just an Irish tradition. We certainly influenced the American tradition, but we didn’t really invent it. Most of our Hallowe’en experiences are shared with our neighbours over in Scotland, the Isle of Man, Wales and parts of England, as well as our mainland European neighbours which is tied in with their St. Martin’s Eve traditions on the 11th of November or 'Old Hallowe’en’ as it was called by some. I do not have the word count to unravel the complete Hallowe’en tangle, but I will spell out the four main distinctive elements which make up the Irish Hallowe’en experience; Food/Harvest, Mumming/Disguise, The Dead/Light and Tricks/Devilment. I will share just one with you - the Mumming/Disguise element. Unlike other parts of the county and country, the Hallowe'en tradition along the north east coast of Wexford where I grew up was very strong. Many of us grew up knowing Hallowe’en as ‘All Hollow's Eve’, ‘All Holland’ or ‘Vizzarding Night’, while in other parts of north Wexford it was known as ‘Blackmen Night’ or ‘Collicking Night’. In other parts of the country they called it Púca Night, Pookie Night, Juggy Night, Snap Apple Night and over in Newfoundland, Colcannon Night.

stories.title: Fionnula Flanagan receives Late Late Show Legend Award
stories.summary: Fionnula Flanagan has been honoured with The Late Late Show Legend Award in recognition of her 60-plus years on stage and screen. The award was presented to the Dubliner by her fellow actors and The Guard co-stars Liam Cunningham and Pat Shortt on Friday night's Late Late Show. "I've never seen a more applicable word than 'legend' for Fionnula Flanagan," said Cunningham. Shortt saluted Flanagan for being a trailblazer for Irish acting talent in Hollywood, winning a Primetime Emmy Award for the miniseries Rich Man, Poor Man in 1976. "There was a great sense of pride watching Fionnula," said Shortt. "I mean, it was an era when - you're going back to the mid-70s, late 70s and that - there was nobody doing it in Hollywood. It was just you, and it was incredible."

stories.title: 3 ways to reduce your taxes in the next three weeks
stories.summary: The scariest moment for many people in Ireland this weekend isn't Halloween – it’s the tax deadline! In reality, the majority of us file online these days, which means the date has been extended from midnight on 31 October to Wednesday 18 November. So there’s still time to reclaim what’s due to you. With three weeks to go, here are three ways you can reduce your taxes before the drop-dead date. Tax relief is a refund of income tax when you’ve incurred certain costs. For example, if you saw your GP last year and paid €75 as a consultation fee, you can claim income tax relief at 20% on that cost, meaning a €15 reduction on your taxes. A huge amount goes unclaimed each year. In fact, last year, Revenue published an estimate that €389 million went unclaimed in 2024. The big area is health expenses, as we’ll see, but there are others, such as rent (including, for example, if you’re supporting a child away from home), some third-level tuition costs, and maintenance payments.

stories.title: EY Ireland's annual revenue grows by 4.4% to €880m
stories.summary: Professional services firm EY Ireland has reported continued growth for its financial year to the end of June 2026. EY Ireland reported annual revenues of €880m on the island of Ireland, an increase of 4.4% on the €843m reported in the previous year. Revenue in the Republic of Ireland reached €810m, an increase of 3.7% on last year's revenue of €781m, it added. The company's headcount across the island stood at more than 5,600 at the end of June 2026, with almost 100 different nationalities working across all areas of the business. It now has 158 Equity Partners across the island of Ireland, including 144 in the Republic of Ireland. During the year, Taoiseach Micheál Martin officially opened its new headquarters at Wilton Park in Dublin, as well as its expanded Cork offices on Lapps Quay.

stories.title: Cullen thrilled as much-changed Leinster run riot
stories.summary: Leo Cullen hailed the "mindset" of his Leinster players as they produced their best performance of the season in a 50-5 hammering of Connacht in Galway. Led by a stunning 20-point haul for Joey Carbery, the defending URC champions dominated from start to finish at Dexcom Stadium as they reeled off a fourth win in a row in all competitions. Both sides were heavily affected by Ireland call-ups this week, with Connacht down eight players and Leinster losing 17, but it was Cullen's side who looked by far the most cohesive, even allowing for 14 changes made by the head coach from last week's win against Munster. "The performance is what you look at first, and I thought there was great commitment in a pretty short week," Cullen said, after his side equalled their biggest ever win away to Connacht. "So huge credit to everyone, the coaches were all excellent in terms of preparing the lads, because we knew there was a lot of changes coming, you get a little bit of a head start last week as well. "I applaud the players in terms of the mindset they had all week, in terms of what they brought to the game.

stories.title: Kate Mulgrew shares Patrick Stewart's Star Trek wisdom
stories.summary: The Galway Bay Murders star Kate Mulgrew has paid tribute to the late Patrick Stewart and the advice he gave her when she began playing Captain Kathryn Janeway on Star Trek: Voyager. "He came in, I think, in the second week I was shooting," she told the host. "I'd just gotten off The Bridge. I'd already lost 52 lbs I was so... I mean, it's nerve-wracking. I was shot out of a cannon. "He came in and, you know, in that gorgeous baritone, helped himself to a coffee. I stepped off The Bridge and I came over and I said, 'How the hell did you do this?' "He said (adopting Patrick Stewart's voice): 'Now, listen to me, and listen to me very clearly. If you invest yourself completely for seven years, as I did, you will be deeply rewarded. So just give it everything you've got'. And that's exactly what I did." "What he was saying was you've got to take a deep breath and dive," Mulgrew explained.

stories.title: Meet the Irish designer dressing Charli XCX, Slayyyter and Adéla
stories.summary: Sínann Fetherston speaks with emerging Irish designer Julia O'Callaghan about the Victorian inspiration behind her work. Having wrapped an internship at Maison Margiela, and with pieces recently spotted on Charli XCX and Adéla, Irish designer Julia O'Callaghan is quickly becoming one to watch. A graduate of the prestigious Central Saint Martins in London, O'Callaghan says that a career in fashion has never been out of the question. Her fascination with the subject, she says, came from her aunt, Hilary O'Kelly, a dress historian and lecturer in Fashion Studies at Dublin's National College of Art and Design. "She taught me how to sew when I was like, four or something," she laughs. "I think she had a motive. That's where I was going to go; I was totally obsessed with it." When the Dublin woman speaks of fashion, she does so with zeal. Her enthrallment to the intricacies behind each stitch makes her role as a designer seem more of a calling than a job.

stories.title: Dublin-based student on brink of Ironman world record
stories.summary: For Dublin-based Thomas Baldauf, 1 November is Guinness Record time, and all it will take is some 14 hours or so to achieve it. The Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland (RCSI) medical student will be in San Juan in Argentina attempting to break a Guinness World Record by becoming the youngest male to complete an Ironman triathlon on six different continents. Fellow American Taeyoung Lee holds the current record after finishing an event in Korea last September aged 21 years 167 days, but if all goes to plan, Baldauf will better him by 82 days. The endurance race - consisting of a 3.8km swim, an 180km bike ride and finally a 42.2km run - has taken Baldauf to Europe (Estonia), Asia (Malaysia), Africa (South Africa), Australia/Oceania (Australia) and North America (Canada). When South America is ticked off, that'll leave just ice sheet-covered Antarctica and, wouldn't you know it, the South Pole hasn't escaped the Ironman craze with Anders Hofman completing the first endurance race there six years ago [his finishing time was 72 hours, 52 minutes and 33 seconds, if you're counting]. Baldauf generally clocks in just over the 14-hour mark - although there was an out-of-nowhere 12:38.51 in Ottawa in August - and ranks highest in swimming, but this record hunt hasn't been about the time, more about the overall accomplishment, with a little bit of family pride thrown in for good measure too.

stories.title: Ireland had highest EU electricity prices in first half
stories.summary: New figures from Eurostat show that Ireland had the highest electricity prices at €0.39 per kWh in the European Union in the first half of this year. It was followed by Germany and Belgium, both with prices of €0.36 per kWh. Eurostat said the lowest prices were recorded in Hungary at €0.11, as well as Malta and Bulgaria - both at €0.13 each. Six countries reported prices above €0.30 per kWh, while five countries recorded prices below €0.20 per kWh, Eurostat noted. Today's figures show that national currency comparisons show strong price movements in the first half of this year compared to the same time last year. Household electricity prices soared by 51.6% in Romania, while they rose by 19.8% in Ireland and by 18.4% in Finland. But some countries recorded sharp decreases, notably Denmark, with prices there falling by 31.7%, while prices in Luxembourg were down 24.1%.

stories.title: Carbery shines as Leinster hammer Connacht in Galway
stories.summary: Leinster's depth of talent proved too good for Connacht as Leo Cullen's side signed off their opening block of the BKT United Rugby Championship by routing Connacht 50-5 at Dexcom Stadium. The defending champions defied woeful weather conditions in Galway, as a mix of old and new faces shone, combining for seven tries and extending their winning run in this fixture to 14 games. Joey Carbery gave a reminder of his class as he orchestrated Leinster's fluid attack, scoring a try among a personal tally of 20 points. Carbery was the only survivor from last week's starting team against Munster, but the province looked cohesive in attack throughout, and the out-half dovetailed brilliantly with some of Leinster's younger talent, as Todd Lawlor and Connor Fahy caught the eye. They were 21-5 ahead by half time, Gus McCarthy, Jordan Larmour and Lawlor all crossing, with Dave Heffernan's maul try all Connacht could offer, while further scores from Max Deegan, Carbery, Ciaran Mangan and Fintan Gunne saw them match their biggest ever win away to Connacht. A third URC win in a row leaves Leinster well-placed heading into the international break, while Stuart Lancaster's Connacht came crashing back to earth, as they looked lost without their eight Ireland squad members.

stories.title: US judge blocks Justice Dept over election directives
stories.summary: A US federal judge has temporarily blocked the Justice Department from threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution if they fail to comply with its directives on processing ballots. The order by Judge Trina Thompson in the Northern District of California deals a setback to Trump administration efforts to restrict voting by people it says might not be US citizens in the 3 November midterm elections. The harshly worded temporary restraining order was issued in response to a case brought by a labour union and civil rights groups against the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security. "Defendants shall not threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by Defendants to be ineligible to vote," Judge Thompson wrote. The judge also ruled that Justice Department officials "shall not threaten state or local election officials and workers with criminal prosecution for failure to comply" with such demands. President Donald Trump's Republican Party is at risk of losing its control of Congress in next Tuesday's elections, and critics have accused his administration of trying to cast doubt on electoral results.

stories.title: Rovers celebrate league title despite Dundalk defeat
stories.summary: Shamrock Rovers collected the SSE Airtricity League Men's Premier Division title but Dundalk spoilt the party somewhat at Oriel Park after coming from a goal down at the break to claim their first home win since 29 May. Things were looking good for Stephen Bradley’s side when they were gifted an opener courtesy of a Rob Cornwall own goal on 23 minutes but a Daryl Horgan equaliser early in the second half followed by a Cian Dillon double against his old club ensured a positive end to the season for Ciarán Kilduff’s side, who had won just one of their previous 14 league matches prior to this. The victory ensures last season’s First Division winners finish the season in sixth, but it was still a night for the Hoops, who lifted their sixth title in seven years in front of a packed away end afterwards. Just like last season when Sligo Rovers crashed the party at Tallaght Stadium on trophy lift night, this defeat won’t worry Bradley a jot, as he rotated his side throughout the second half, calling the likes of Graham Burke and captain Pico Lopes ashore before half-time. Indeed, despite the defeat - their ninth in their last 13 visits to Oriel - the Hoops end the year two points better off than last year and are still the team to beat with one eye on 2027. The celebrations almost started early for Rovers when Burke attempted to lob Peter Cherrie inside the opening four minutes from about 45 yards out only for his effort to drift to the left and wide.

stories.title: Who is going to be haunted by the US midterms?
stories.summary: The numbers couldn't be clearer. Americans are eager to have their say on the future direction of the country. As of last night, more than 48 million people had cast a ballot at early voting stations or by post. The figures are significantly outpacing those recorded at the same point in the last midterm election. The sharpest increases are in states with fiercely competitive Senate races that could determine which party controls the chamber. Just look at Texas. The Republican-leaning Lone Star state has dominated national and international headlines for its tight US Senate, House and governor races. More than 6.3 million Texans voted during the first seven days of early voting. That's compared with 4.2 million people at the same point four years ago.

stories.title: Blues bounce into cup decider with Tolka Park success
stories.summary: Waterford bounced into Sunday's Club Orange FAI Cup final with Derry City thanks to a 3-2 victory to beat Shelbourne 3-2 and secure their Premier Division status. That would have been unlikely, with Drogheda United requiring an eight-goal swing to send them to a relegation play-off, but goals from Evan McLaughlin, Pádraig Among and Tommy Lonergan removed all uncertainty. The Reds had threatened to spoil the party atmosphere among the visitors as they led through eight minutes thanks to a wonderstrike from captain Kerr McInroy. Waterford turned the tables either side of the break as McLaughlin forced home from close range before Amond’s bullet header put the visitors in an unlikely lead. Another terrific long range strike, this time from JJ Lunney, brought the sides even on the scoreboard as Shels looked to sign off their season on a high. Lonergan was to have the final say with just three minutes remaining on the clock as he met sub Joe Ashton’s cross to nod home and finish as the Premier Division’s top scorer with 16.

stories.title: Poland's president returns as court crisis escalates
stories.summary: Polish President Karol Nawrocki turned back ⁠to Poland while en route to Senegal after a far-right ally was suspended as head of the country's top court, escalating a battle with Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government over control of the judiciary. Yesterday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska had suspended Bogdan Swieczkowski, the tribunal's president and an appointee of Mr Tusk's far-right predecessor, and was now in charge of the court. Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the tribunal last night amid a heavy police presence, while right-wing politicians addressed the crowd accusing Mr Tusk's government of carrying out a coup ‌against the court. "At a moment ⁠like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," Mr Nawrocki said on X. A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognise appointees put forward by the other side. Mr Tusk, writing on ‌X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors - the Law and Justice Party - of ⁠subverting.

stories.title: Sun Goddess gives Aidan O'Brien record breaking win
stories.summary: Sun Goddess confirmed herself as a two-year-old out of the ordinary with a clear-cut win Breeders' Cup Juvenile Fillies Turf at Keeneland Seen by many as the banker of the two-day meeting, she already had three Group Ones in Europe to her credit but she had to contend with the journey to America and stall nine. However, Ryan Moore got her out of the stalls sharply and across to the inside in the perfect position just behind the leader whereas her main market rival, Francis-Henri Graffard’s Amusingly, had to settle at the rear of the field. As soon as Moore kicked clear early in the straight the race was over as a contest and once again it was left to Joseph O’Brien’s Green Empress to chase her home, the fourth time she has been second to the winner this year. Johnny Murtagh’s Curracloe ran a fine race to finish third while Amusingly made late gains under Colin Keane for fourth. Joseph O’Brien’s Alwaysanangel finished fifth in a clean sweep for the Europeans. It was Aidan O’Brien’s 22nd Breeders’ Cup winner, meaning he has now had more winners at the meeting than anybody else, having been previously tied with Bob Baffert.

stories.title: Three men behind plot to bomb Galway mosque jailed
stories.summary: Three men who were part of a self-styled terrorist organisation that planned to blow up a mosque in Galway last year have been jailed at the Special Criminal Court as the presiding judge told them they have "brought shame on us all." 36-year-old Garrett Pollock of Kilhorne Greene, Annalong, Co Down was sentenced to ten and a half years with the last year suspended. 34-year-old Darren Gorman of O'Moore Place in Portlaoise was sentenced eight years with the last year suspended and 39-year-old Karolis Peckauskas with an address at Newfoundwell Road, Drogheda, Co Louth was sentenced to eight years in prison with the last year suspended. All three pleaded guilty to attempting to engage in a terrorist activity, to firebomb the Maryam Mosque on the Monivea Road in Galway between 4 and 5 November 2025, an offence aggravated by hatred. Pollock also pleaded guilty to possession of an explosive substance which was found in four glass jars concealed in a hidden drawer in his van on 4 November 2025. The three also threatened to attack anyone involved in mosques, IPAS centres, hotels and other accommodation for people seeking international protection.

A spokesperson for the PSNI said: "Police are investigating a report of an assault on a member of the clergy at St Patrick's Cathedral in Armagh."

stories.title: Hegarty and O'Donoghue win Player of the Year awards
stories.summary: Mayo's Ryan O'Donoghue was selected as the 2026 Footballer of the Year, while Limerick's Gearóid Hegarty was crowned Hurler of the Year for the second time at the PwC All-Star awards in the RDS tonight. O'Donoghue, who was awarded Man of the Match for his display in the All-Ireland final, saw off competition from his fellow nominees, three-time Footballer of the Year David Clifford and Mayo team-mate Jack Carney. O'Donoghue is the third Mayo player to the win the Footballer of the Year after Lee Keegan in 2016 and Andy Moran in 2017. Meanwhile, Limerick half-forward Hegarty has become only the third multiple winner of the GAA/GPA Hurler of the Year award, earning the nod ahead of his team-mate Diarmaid Byrnes and two-time nominee Brian Hayes. The 32-year old wing-forward joins Kilkenny's Henry Shefflin (2002, 2006, 2012) and his Limerick team-mate Cian Lynch (2018, 2021) as the only three players to have won the award more than once since it was launched in 1995. Brian Corcoran, DJ Carey and Brian Whelehan were also multiple winners if one includes the pre-existing Texaco Hurler of the Year awards, which ran from 1958 until 2012.

stories.title: Toll hikes for motorway, Port Tunnel users from January
stories.summary: The cost of tolls on most of the country's roads are set to rise from 1 January, Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) has confirmed. Among the roads to see increases will be the M50, the country's busiest road, and Port Tunnel in Dublin, with all categories of vehicles on the M50 seeing a hike. The toll for cars using the M50 will increase by 10 cent per trip for motorists who have a tag or video account (to €2.70 for tag accounts and €3.30 for video accounts). However, motorists using the M50 without any account will see their toll rise by 20c to €4 per trip. There will also be an increase of 10c for all of the country's Public-Private Partnership (PPP) toll roads - except for the M3 Clonee to Kells toll, which remains unchanged. The PPP increases cover tolls on the M1, N6, M7/M8, M8, N18-LT, and N25WF.

She pointed jurors to his 2007 book, where he discussed his "birthright orgasm", and a 2017 interview Mr Brand gave when he referred to women as "amusements" in a "playground of orgasms". stories.title: Champions Limerick dominate All-Star selection
stories.summary: All-Ireland SHC champions Limerick secured nine spots on this year's PwC All-Stars hurling team, matching their second biggest haul during this remarkable era. John Kiely's side, who regained the All-Ireland title in emphatic style after a three-year gap, completely dominate the middle third of the team, monopolising the half-back line and half-forward line spots, with wing-forward Gearóid Hegarty scooping the Player of the Year award for the second time in his career. Every player from No. 4 to 12 comes from the All-Ireland champions, with the exception of Galway midfielder Tom Monaghan. Overall, just four counties are represented, with All-Ireland finalists Galway nabbing three spots, while the losing semi-finalists Cork and Clare have two and one respectively. The Limerick contingent contains three first-time All-Stars, with Adam English taking a midfield berth alongside Monaghan, while half-forwards Aidan O'Connor and Cathal O'Neill are included in the team alongside Hegarty, who takes his fifth All-Star in total. Kyle Hayes, at wing-back, claims his sixth All-Star altogether, drawing him level with Joe McKenna as the most decorated Limerick hurler in the history of the awards.

stories.title: Polish riot police deployed after court chief suspended
stories.summary: Polish President Karol Nawrocki has turned back his plane en route to Senegal after police entered the premises of Poland's top court and its president was suspended. "At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," he said on X. Police said officers entered the premises of the Constitutional Tribunal after incidents outside the court, including the throwing of dangerous objects at police. The tribunal said on its website that the court's president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, had been suspended. A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution. Earlier this year, Mr Nawrocki, an ally of Poland's former nationalist government of the Law and Justice or PiS party, refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Mr Swieczkowski, who was a deputy justice minister under PiS, declined to allow judges elected by the current parliamentary majority to assume their duties.

stories.title: Commissioner 'trampling over rights' of gardaí, says GRA
stories.summary: The president of the Garda Representative Association has called on the Garda Commissioner to "desist from trampling over the rights" of gardaí regarding overtime and days off. It comes as rank-and-file gardaí announced a plan yesterday to engage in five days of work-to-rule action next month, coinciding with a major EU Presidency meeting of leaders in Dublin on 13 November. The work-to-rule, which is being staged over dissatisfaction with garda working conditions, will commence on Tuesday 10 November and run until Saturday 14 November. This includes the European Political Convention on 12 November, as well as the informal meeting of the EU heads of state or government on 13 November. The GRA has accused the Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly and garda management of breaching the Working Time Agreement and the European Working Time Directive. He said two years ago, the Garda Commissioner’s office and leadership time were part signatories to the Working Time Agreement, which he said, is a set of rules so that both sides have fairness.

stories.title: Bakhurst confident €20m funding shortfall will be secured
stories.summary: Mr Bakhurst said while it "was a bit of a shock" to suddenly be told of the shortfall just hours before the Budget was announced, he predicted the situation would be resolved. He said he wished Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O'Donovan all the best as he recovers from illness, saying this would not impede progress in securing the funding. "The Secretary General's currently running the department in the absence of Patrick and the officials, working hard, we're giving them the information they want," he said. "I said it was unconscionable to take part last year. I think it would have been very, very difficult to take part next year and that's why we took the decision early, given the ongoing conditions in Gaza and West Bank and other parts of the region and given where the Irish audience is. "So, I don't think it's going to be easy to go back until there's a very significant change on the ground or until Israel is not in the Eurovision," Mr Bakhurst said. He acknowledged there were complex implications to such decisions.
